reviews.review: Engaging and compelling, everyone should try it!

I bought this game months ago because it was cheap (I believe it was on sale at the time) and completely forgot about it until now. I went into this game with not knowing what to expect, and now I am addicted to it. I think it is a perfect game for those who like to find clues and solve mysteries. I can see how this could be boring for some other people since all you do is clicking different buttons on the screen to find clues. However, the back stories are very interesting and I think that alone make this game worth playing.

I do have some criticisms for this game though. When I was trying to complete the first chapter, the game kept telling I have one more clue to find, I looked up guides online and saw that I already found everything. I figured it was a bug and had to restart the chapter. Some of the voice acting also feel a bit unnatural, it's almost like the voice actors were just reading from the script which kind of threw me off. In a few dialogues, what the voice actors said also did not match the subtitle, which is fine if they have the same meaning but for example, there is one part where the subtitle said "hacker" while the voice actor said "leader" which feels a bit off since the character we play as isn't really a "leader". I am also not too crazy about the illustrations, some of the characters' anatomy look weird and not consistent (when there are 3 illustrations of the same character from different angles, they almost look like 3 different people) I do like how painterly it looks but in some areas they used actual photos with a filter while some of them they kept the painterly illustrations which is a bit odd.

Nevertheless for me, it was a game worth playing and I definitely would be interested to check out the DLCs and the next game after this one.

Why does the 100% achievement for Chapter 3 have a 51% completion rate among players? This is the most completed game I’ve ever seen.

There’s something unusual about the gameplay, it makes you want to take a break, but then you come back for the next chapter.

I really liked the story and the mechanics. Personally I found it a little hard, but well figuring out the clues is whats fun of the game. Definitely recommend it if you like detective games with a side of hacking.

There is a lot to like, but overall I wouldn't _recommend_ this game.

First off, in my perspective, timers ruin most everything that could be fun. Life is busy, interruptions pop up. In this game, one cannot pause and there's not a lot of time allowed for dilly dallying. Always seems a silly way of trying to make something challenging, having to do it faster. The timed parts are simple enough, and seem to be re-doable, but they're not enjoyable that way.  Nearer the end in particular are some puzzles that would be much more enjoyable without a timer or at least with a pause button.

What possibly contributed to souring my experience 
I wound up having to play a bunch of the game over twice, because first I couldn't make any of the boxes on the screen move, during a timed event. After click click clicking all around, I restarted. The game seemed like it was picking up just before the timed part, but nothing I did could trigger the timed part. nothing would happen. So, I restarted from a manual save point. Then, before I caught back up to where I had been, I inadvertently closed a window that then wouldn't open again, and the game proceeded as though I had made a different choice, so I went back to my manual save point again because I didn't want that. Through that experience, I became more aware how tedious the copying and pasting can be.

It is very close to being a game I would recommend and I wouldn't tell anybody not to get it. The price isn't at all bad. I just got too irritated at not being able to pause those timed parts to complete it.

This is a fun game for those of us who enjoy snooping and testing our deduction skills. One thing that really needs to be improved is the English translation of a lot of the text. There were a ton of grammatical errors that made certain things difficult to understand, and a lot of the phrasing came across as stilted and odd. Despite that, it's still an enjoyable experience.

This game had a solid idea, but the execution is a complete disaster. The UI is an absolute nightmare—it feels less like you're playing and more like you're struggling to get it to work as you intended. Instead of immersing you, it just makes you want to slam your head into a brick wall. You're endlessly clicking, hoping for something to highlight and when it finally does? It’s barely relevant to the information you want t look for.

And the worst part? The game presents obvious clues in fragmented parts, but it doesn’t let you connect them until it decides you’ve "earned it". You can see the bigger picture, but it keeps those pieces hidden, forcing you to waste time hunting for stuff that’s already right in front of you. It’s like the game is deliberately holding back info, making you run in circles just to unlock something that should’ve been obvious from the start.

To top it all off, you can’t even explore anything the game doesn’t deem necessary, no matter how much you know it should be. Even when you’re certain something else is important, the game stops you, forcing you to stick to its narrow path. It’s like being told exactly where to stand and when to look, even though you can see a whole branch of information that just "not related" .

Is this just me being picky about how the game should be or should I try to give it another shot?

This game is not a hacking-themed command-based or typing game, but rather a puzzle/visual novel. It has an overarching plot spanning five chapters, each with its own self-contained story. While the main plot felt predictable and leaned on surface level philosophical tropes (which had me rolling my eyes), I found the individual chapter stories far more engaging due to their focused and contained themes.

I burned out before finishing the final chapter. Still, I’d recommend it as a solid experience. it just didn’t quite make an impact for me to continue.

Cyber Manhunt is a take on an Orwell style game, but it lacks the polish and quality of those titles. Sometimes you can find a piece of information that you need (for example, a character's name) earlier in a chapter, but the game won't let you 'learn' it until you reach a later point because it isn't the specific place where the game wants you to collect that information. Certain dialogue choices are vague and their outcomes are unpredictable. Sometimes the game will ask you to provide specific information that you collected (or information that the game never clearly gave) but won't let you access your 'notes'.

There are a few interesting minigames scattered throughout, but some of them give a strict time limit and vague guidance as to what you need to do. Failure just sets you back a short time, but in some instances you're forced to sit through unskippable dialogue scenes to get back to the minigame.

There are a lot of good ideas here, and the chapters and overall story are fairly interesting, but the overall presentation makes this more of a frustrating experience than a fun one.
Great game, really fun!

I really wanted to like this game, but it felt like the game was fighting me for that enjoyment. I really liked similar games like Orwell, The Roottrees are Dead, and Obra Dinn, but this game lacks a significant amount of polish. Some of the dialogue options are vague and nonsensical, and some of the clues required to progress are vague and require multiple re-reads to collect information you already know. A lot of this could probably have been cleared up with a better English translation of the game. I think it shows promise, but it definitely needs work.

I really enjoyed the story, there is lots of twists and turns! I really liked how the chapters were integrated and built up the story. I bought both of the paid DLCs and I really enjoyed both of them. To get the whole story I think you need to buy the Hello World DLC (It is basically a prologue for this game). The puzzles for this game I would say are very linear in difficulty, and in my opinion do not get harder as you progress through the story, which can either be taken as a positive or negative. 

Overall, the main story + Hello World + Home Sweet Home DLCs gave me around 13 hours of playtime, which for the price is around a pound an hour. Even though I really enjoyed the puzzles, I would recommend the game based on the story alone! And I will be buying the sequel, so take of that as you will.

Probably should have played this before Cyber Manhunt 2, which is much more polished in terms of the UI, art, translation and voice acting. But this was still a worthy predecessor in general, and it was fun to retroactively come across familiar characters and uncover snippets of their pasts, though I liked Van much better in CM2. In any case, the detective/hacking parts were still among my favorite aspects, even if the minigames are harder here, and the story was solid. If the developers ever make another of these, I'd still absolutely play it.

[Side note: While playing the DLC "Home Sweet Home" watch out for the final minigame crashing. Not sure if it was just me, but halfway through logging into the Bird's Eye system the game stopped responding for ~15 min so I had to exit, preventing me from getting the final achievement. Hopefully this will be fixed soon, but I don't feel like replaying the entire chapter just to try and get those last 2 minutes back.]

What an incredibly unique and engaging game this is. I would normally advise anyone who is even a little interested to simply go in blind, but if you want a short description of the moment-to-moment: imagine a point and click adventure game, where you must locate certain information to progress, using internet search engines and personal e-mails as your setting.

If there is a flaw in the 7 hours/2 chapters that I've played, it's that sometimes you will be timed while searching for "key information" in a designated area. You often aren't told exactly what you're looking for, leading to, essentially, a pixel hunt where you sift through all the data as fast as you can, hoping you get lucky before time runs out. It's actually pretty effective at building tension, but failing often means a reset to a checkpoint that's JUST far back enough to be annoying, but not ruinous. Given this, for the love of all that's holy, leave the "hints" option turned on in settings. As far as I can tell, it doesn't hold your hand or spoil any deductions you need to make. It simply highlights relevant text when your mouse hovers over it, which I find invaluable.

Honestly, this hiccup is a small blemish on an otherwise fascinating and truly cool game. The gameplay is a form of social information gathering and hacking that I've never seen done in this way, nor organized as well as it is. You have all the info you need to deduce your next step at any time in your onscreen folder, and getting stuck, in my experience, is due to a lack of thoroughness on my part. Also, the stories really deliver some truly good gut-punches (again, of the two main chapters I've played). Maybe I'm a sap, but the conclusions always left me feeling bad, in the "best" way possible. On a related note, the translation is pretty solid. Some phrasing can come off as odd or unnatural, but the meaning of the sentence is never confused. Awkward from time to time, but perfectly understandable.

An ok attempt at whatever this genre is, it's no The Operator, but it's (mostly) playable and very rough around the edges, being riddled with terrible ESL dialogue that ChatGPT could've done a better job at generating. This game is translated from Chinese so that accounts for some of those issues, but worse are that some of the "puzzles" are just incomprehensible nonsense based off of bad information the game gives you. In places like the "symbols" password or the phone unlock pattern for Jim's phone you will basically have to use a guide because you aren't given correct information, or an indicator that you have bad information and need to work around it. You will also require a guide for the later public opinion "game" which can be found on Steam, because it is unplayable as the Engrish describing each topic makes it incomprehensible as to whether it's good or bad to promote.  

The voice acting and art are also not great, two other aspects that quite frankly would've been handled better by AI, and the menu options have text that sometimes don't fit their graphics or are hidden behind them. Overall the presentation and feel is very janky mid-2000s but I'm giving it a yes anyway because I like this genre and at least an attempt was made. At the time of this writing there is already a sequel out so hopefully some of these issues were ironed out, but that remains to be seen.

(2) The function of having to gather all clues before being able to proceed makes sense; however, if you somehow forget to scan something like a Toothbook ID, you just can't progress and have no idea what to do. But these problems don't make it a bad game. It's still really fun to play, even though I recommend playing it with a guide if you have problems.

I enjoy Orwell and other games in this vein. My main issue here is that it's tedious. It doesn't show you which information it wants you to click on until you mouse over it. The result was me being in a place where I knew all the answers and had solved everything, but wasn't allowed to end the level because I had missed clicking on some piece of information somewhere. I looked at important pieces of information multiple times, and eventually found that the piece I had missed was something that was only slightly relevant to the situation at hand. 

In other words- it didn't make me feel like I was solving puzzles. It made me feel like I was trying every single option whether it made sense or not, because that was the only way to progress. I give Cyber Manhunt a middle B. It's a fun investigation game that is similar to Orwell and Analogue: A Hate Story where you piece together the plot by using "hacking," or really Hollywood-style hacking in between social engineering.

The gameplay suffers a bit for its loop, in which the majority of your time is spent looking through in-game social media logs of your subjects. That's a fun premise, but the game proceeds by having you click on relevant lines of text. When you hover your cursor over lines you can "collect" to add to your case file, the lines turn red, but otherwise there is no indication which bits are relevant. There are many times early on I just missed the lines in question, and so I spent the last few chapter meticulously mousing over EVERYTHING so I didn't miss anything, but I STILL missed things. It was a little frustrating and I had to use a guide a couple times to find what I had overlooked, even though I read everything.

More frustrating than that though are the mini-games. Usually when doing something more intense than reading, you're playing a mini-game to hack a system or reason out a situation. For the most part these mini-games aren't difficult and I appreciate the variety. However, in later chapters the mini-games start getting time limits, and some of these are unnecessarily harsh. A particular hacking mini-game in Chapter 5 nearly made me rage quit, and even with a video tutorial from YouTube, I was really struggling to get past it. Maybe I'm just a slow reader, but I think it's just less-than-good game design.

The developer seemed to understand those criticisms too because in the Home Sweet Home DLC there aren't any time limits, and in Hello World there is only one mini-game with a time limit that's [i]incredibly[/i] generous. Also in the DLCs, the mini-games can be straight up skipped. I wish that had been in the base game.

Luckily, all mini-games and gameplay loop tedium are absolutely overshadowed by the excellent story. All seven chapters (DLC included) had great twists and turns. All the cases are connected in subtle ways, and almost no one ended up how they began. All the characters were complex, and the writers absolutely nailed social media posts, including strangers of all genders uncomfortably randomly hitting on strangers in their own feeds. And what starts off as a "simple" matter of investigation eventually spirals into sci-fi and metaphysical questions. I loved it.

The English translation is unfortunately wonky, and there are typos or "just doesn't sound right" issues in just about every other sentence. There's also some polish issues where the voice acting doesn't quite match up with what's on the screen, like the script changed after the line were recorded. Even so, the translation is good enough that you can follow what's going on and there's nothing more egregious than mixing up pronouns. But man, if the story had been run through a native English speaker/writer before being released, this would have been an [i]incredible[/i] story.

The music is awesome as well, and really sets the mood, but the story really caries the game. I'm excited to try the sequel now, though I'm hoping the gameplay loop for Cyber Manhunt 2 is less tedious.

This game is pretty good. The english isn't perfect but it's good enough. I have to give a warning: I'm not a puzzle person. I suck at puzzles. I was able to do a good portion on my own and used a guide for the rest. There are very dark themes, there's mentions of SA and animal abuse, it's disturbing. The story is absolutely fantastic and sucked me in. THAT SAID. The puzzle at the end are absolutely ridiculous. I get it's the end, there's a big climax to the story. I spent well over an hour trying to do the end puzzles WITH A GUIDE. They are timed, it was impossible for me to get the good ending, I didn't have enough time. I had to settle for the general ending, which I almost cried because you still have to solve a few more puzzles before you get the end.

So I say I'd recommend this if you enjoy puzzles and a challenge. Maybe not so much if you're more of a casual gamer. They do have a "simple" mode on like a puzzle at the end if you failed too much. I was happy to finally beat the game. I was glad to see the end story and it hooks you to want to play more. I'm on the fence about the DLC since the puzzles.. UGH. I got this bundled with the sequel so I'll try that. I wouldn't say this game is a definite thumbs up. I'd probably give a neutral rating if there was one.

I would like to first thank the dev for this game and for having taken the time to translate the game  (whatever may be the tools used for it) so we, non-chinese players, could venture into your universe. I've bought this game along with its DLC and the second game that is currently in Early access (I'll start that one when I've got some time).

But let's jump in the meat of the review. 

1)  I can't start without addressing the main issue of this game, for us non-chinese readers/speakers : the translation. Many things have been said about it and while the two DLC's do display a better text than the main game, let's be honest and say that it's the major con of the software. 

I would like to tone this concern down in regard with my earlier praise to the dev for translating it, but nonetheless it led me to check for guides on Steam and videos on youtube to solve some problems that were either due to a vague translation or to more problematic issues as I'll develop below.

2) Voice acting.... not necessary and not very welcome either. You've got a range of icons to tell us that we're listening to a phone call, it's not like we need to listen to anything in particular. Let's take the good examples of Orwell and Song of Farca that don't have any voice acting and yet have a great atmosphere, great writing, etc. And also, no option to mute voices only, Or you mute all the sounds (music being dealt with apart from it) or you have to listen to .... quite robotic or emotionless or otherwise misplayed dialogues. Again, DLC's level up the game a little more on that matter.

3) My main concern is definitely the lack of "respect" that I felt sometimes during the game. I understand that the dev team is very small, but then select what you display on screen, please. And make it, if not useful, at least usable. 
   - many web articles are just there for lore purpose, nothing else ;
   - tapped phone calls received through mail are not always usable to make the case progress ; 
   - some hinted leads are dead ends from the start, no way to investigate them ;
   - No way to direct call people we know the phone numbers.... ;
   - Sometimes, the chuncks of info that you have to select make little sense, mostly due to the translation. Why should I 
      select an obvious conclusion to a drama (for instance : "I'm alone in the world now that they're gone") and not the fact 
      themselves (for example : "They died in a car accident last month") ? ;
      Ok, it's not always that simplistic, but it's sometimes the case and in the end, it becomes more of a clicker game where 
      you hunt down info at random than an actual investigation. Again, respect your player intelligence or try to have a 
      better translated and adapted script, because while I'm grateful to you for your effort, it was a bit underwhelming...;
   - maybe my main grip here : you often have to select the information in a particular document and not anywhere else. 
      And that is a huge concern of mine. Let's say you see that NPC 1 got divorced while skimming through a web article. You could extract the data here and add it to the share folder, right ? No, you will have to wait for the same info to appear on an obscure Darknet-ish forum or on social medias, etc. Which is.... not unseen before but still annoying. 

Do respect your players. Be conscious of your own limitations and restrict our freedom of action right from the start instead of giving us the illusion of "freedom of action". Again, not unseen before in this kind of games and others genres. Indeed, it has been a recurring pattern since the beginning of gaming, but... maybe there are elegant ways to deal with it. Again, Orwell dealt with it quite nicely by focusing on what was relevant for us, for the story, for the game. Another thing that can be done is letting us "phone" the characters and just letting them or not answering, or blocking us, or just repeating the same automatic response. It would still tell us that it is a dead end, but at least we wouldn't feel like heavily disabled persons unable to put 2 and 2 and take action. 

4) Good writing, good story, good characters. I liked all the cases and the general story. Nothing new under the sky, but well done. The themes were indeed a bit stressful and character writing was deep enough for me to like/love/dislike/hate them and how corrupt or mischievous they can be. Good thriller all in all. Maybe the last DLC was a bit underwhelming. the tower-defence mini-game was interesting though !

5) Music, like voice acting, was a bit redundant, I quickly muted it and put my own in the background. The problem was the same with Song of Farca but at least you could change the track before muting it completely. Orwell did handle it better with a soft lift-like music. 


Ok, I talked too much.

TL;DR => buy it both because it's a good game and to support its dev(s). Despite the caveats I mentioned, I still mostly enjoyed my journey in this universe and will launch the second game when I get time. both gameplay DLC (the only paid DLC, that is) are of good value. "Home Sweet Home" being the better story-wise and the second DLC being better gameplay-wise (because of the mini tower-defence game ^^). 

Regards

Cyber Manhunt plunges players into the gritty and morally ambiguous world of cyber investigation. As an investigator, you use hacking, social engineering, and deduction skills to uncover hidden truths behind various cases. The game's strengths lie in its immersive narrative and realistic depiction of the internet's darker corners.

Pros:

Compelling Storyline: Each case is engaging, with twists that keep you hooked.
Realistic Mechanics: The hacking and investigative processes feel authentic, enhancing immersion.
Ethical Dilemmas: The game forces you to confront tough moral choices, adding depth to the gameplay.

Cons:

Steep Learning Curve: The mechanics can be challenging for newcomers, potentially leading to frustration.
Pacing Issues: Some parts of the game feel slow, which can disrupt the overall flow. 
Making a mistake while in a dialogue section requires you to sit through it all again because you can't skip dialogue. 

Overall, Cyber Manhunt offers a fun experience for fans of investigative and narrative-driven games.

If you like any type of detective game, you will ADORE this game, trust me. Yes, it can be considered "tedious" at times (though I really didn't see it that way), and can sometimes require going back if you want to 100%, but the payoff for investing your interest in this game will NOT fail you.

This game will make your jaw drop at least 10 times while playing it. It will blow your mind, make you question the government and your own password security, and give you so many open-ended questions that you genuinely can just sit with the ideas it gives for days afterwards and still be pondering.

I feel like the people who criticise this game for not being more like Orwell miss what that game lacks, which this game does well. Not every piece of information is a clue to click. To actually understand the world, not just progress the story, you have to read the articles, search things that aren't in a hint but you think could be relevant, read up on people 2 or 3 chapters before they become relevant. This game is so, SO well done and I'm begging you to give it a chance.

Also, for any gripes you have with gameplay, I promise you that the sequel they have in early access (which includes 3/5 of the game already), solves so many of those problems, the dev's are for sure listening and improving and believe me, this game is worth the investment ENTIRELY.
